Havasupai

The Havasupai Tribe’s introduction to Supai emphasizes water and cultivated food. This starting path adds a Havasupai-informed research framework and an attributed public account of Ethel Jack’s advocacy, connecting community life, environmental inquiry and twentieth-century history.

01

Identity and context

The Havasupai Tribe has enduring relationships with the Grand Canyon region and Havasu Canyon.

Read the sources [1] naair.arizona.edu

02

A path for deeper reading

Focus the next stage of research on: Havasupai community perspectives, language, land and contemporary tribal government. The sources below are selected reading paths; their authorship, dates and community scope should guide how they are used.

Read the sources [1] naair.arizona.edu [2] native-languages.org [3] Carletta Tilousi and Jo Ellen Hinck / U.S. Geological Survey

03

Water, food and Supai

The Tribe describes Supai through Havasu Baaja, the People of the Blue Green Waters, and through spring water supporting corn, squash and beans. This community account gives the waterfall photograph a specific setting, while the 1972 image remains a dated landscape rather than a picture of current access conditions.

Read the sources [4] Havasupai Tribe

04

Ethel Jack and the work of advocacy

NPS follows Ethel Jack’s basketry, her family’s experiences of displacement and her work seeking the return of Havasupai lands. It connects her Washington advocacy with the 1975 return. The account draws partly on published recollections; it is a route into that history, not independent inspection of the interviews or legislation.

Read the sources [5] National Park Service

05

Whose concerns shape a research model?

Tilousi and Hinck’s USGS report explains why risk models should include Havasupai perspectives and uses of resources. The introduction also says other Tribal applications would need to reflect their own knowledge systems. It describes a research framework, not measured exposure outcomes or health advice.

Read the sources [3] Carletta Tilousi and Jo Ellen Hinck / U.S. Geological Survey

Publication: 2024-02-01

Carletta Tilousi and Jo Ellen Hinck explain how Havasupai perspectives can change environmental-risk research questions and exposure models.

Scope: Actual title/authors, first-posted and revised dates, Acknowledgments, Abstract and complete Introduction. Later detailed cultural/ceremonial sections, figures and appendices were not reviewed or reproduced.

Native Art and Activism — selected Ethel Jack and Havasupai advocacy account ↗

The Havasupai-focused section follows basket maker Ethel Jack’s advocacy and family experience of displacement, ending with the 1975 land return.

Inspection: Content reviewed for the stated scope

Scope: Actual Havasupai/Ethel Jack body, reader lines 55–60, and its citation to Betty Leavengood, Grand Canyon Women, 2014, pp 195–196. Other artist sections were encountered separately, not counted as Havasupai history.

Review recorded: October 28, 2026

Access note: Normal HTTP 200 public body read. Underlying biography, personal interviews and original legislation uninspected. Memories and the agency’s historical interpretation stay attributed; acreage and present title are not independently established.
